title: Word transformation (doublets)
label: idb
statement:
Given:

• dictionary
• start word
• end word

Each transformation changes exactly one character and the resulting word must exist in the dictionary.

Return minimum number of transformations.

Example:

APE -> APT -> OPT -> OAT -> MAT -> MAN

Output:

5

Follow-ups:
• Convert to an online service with minimal latency
• Will cycles be output?
• What if letters can be added or removed?
provenance: Supplied by you from InterviewDB — the statement above is **verbatim**. Corroboration: InterviewDB + 2 independent reports of Word Ladder.
clarify: The start word need not be in the dictionary; the end word must be.
The dictionary is static in the base problem.

flaw.ctx: The assistant produced this. Later a user reported: "Distance is right, but the queue holds about twice as many entries as there are cells."
flaw.answer: Cells are marked visited on **dequeue**, so a cell can be enqueued once per neighbour before it is processed. **7,081 enqueues for 3,600 cells** on a 60×60 grid; on a word graph with ~25 neighbours per node the factor is ~25×.

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given:
> 
> • dictionary
> • start word
> • end word
> 
> Each transformation changes exactly one character and the resulting word must exist in the dictionary.
> 
> Return minimum number of transformations.
> 
> Example:
> 
> APE -> APT -> OPT -> OAT -> MAT -> MAN
> 
> Output:
> 
> 5
> 
> Follow-ups:
> • Convert to an online service with minimal latency
> • Will cycles be output?
> • What if letters can be added or removed?

A dictionary is secretly a graph. Two words are neighbours if they differ in exactly one position. You are asked for the shortest path between two of them, walking only through real words.

The number of single-character changes on the shortest chain, or a sentinel if no chain exists.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| The start word need not be in the dictionary; the end word must be. | LeetCode 127 makes the same choice. If the start must also be present, that is one validation line. If the **end** need not be, the question is unanswerable — you could never legally arrive. |
| Case and alphabet are consistent. | The example is uppercase. Mixed case would need normalising, and the wildcard index would have to be built on the normalised form or it silently misses neighbours. |
| The answer counts edges. | Fixed by the supplied example: six words, output 5. **This is where LeetCode differs**, so state it. |
| The dictionary is static in the base problem. | The online-service follow-up makes it dynamic, which is why the index is built behind a method rather than inline in the constructor. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The words are not the problem. **Finding the neighbours is the problem**, and that is the whole question.

Once you see that two words are adjacent when they differ in one position, the search is textbook BFS. But how do you find the neighbours of `APE`? The obvious way is to compare it against every word in the dictionary: O(N · L) per expansion, which at N = 50,000 makes each step of the search a scan of the whole dictionary.

The trick is to **index by wildcard**. For each word, generate the patterns you get by blanking each position in turn — `APE` gives `*PE`, `A*E`, `AP*` — and store the word under all three. Now two words are neighbours exactly when they share a pattern, so the neighbours of `APE` are the union of three dictionary lookups. Each expansion drops from O(N · L) to O(L) lookups, and the cost moves to a one-off O(N · L) build.

That move — **precompute a canonical key so the expensive comparison becomes a hash lookup** — is the same idea as Q11’s keypad signature and the same idea behind LeetCode 244. It is worth naming as a pattern rather than as a trick for this problem, because it is what makes the online-service follow-up answerable: the build happens once at startup, and every query is then pure BFS over hash lookups.

The second observation is for the follow-up, and it is the same one as Q5: searching from both ends turns `b^d` into `2 · b^(d/2)`. Here the branching factor is genuinely large — each word has up to 25 · L neighbours — so bidirectional BFS matters more than it does on a social graph.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** BFS, and for each word in the frontier scan the entire dictionary looking for words that differ in exactly one position. *O(N² · L) in the worst case — every one of N words compared against all N, at L character comparisons each. O(N) space.*

**Why not good enough.** At N = 50,000 and L = 5 that is over ten billion character comparisons for one query, and it repeats the same comparisons on every query. The useful framing is that the brute force recomputes adjacency **per query** something that is a property of the **dictionary** — and anything that depends only on the dictionary should be computed once. That reframing is what leads to the wildcard index, and it is also exactly the argument the online-service follow-up wants.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | A dictionary, a start word and an end word |
| TRANSFORMATION | Every word is indexed under L wildcard patterns, one per blanked position |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Dictionary<string, List<string>>` from pattern to words; `HashSet<string>` for the dictionary and for visited; `Queue<string>` for the frontier |
| ALGORITHM | Level-by-level BFS, neighbours via L pattern lookups. Bidirectional: expand the smaller frontier and stop when the two searches meet. |
| OUTPUT | The number of transformations, or -1 |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Build: for each dictionary word, for each position, blank it and append the word to that pattern’s list.
- Guard: different lengths → -1; identical words → 0; end word absent → -1.
- Seed the frontier with the start word, mark it visited, `steps = 0`.
- Take the whole level. `steps++`.
- For each word, for each of its L patterns, for each word in that bucket: if it is the end word, return `steps`; if unseen, mark and queue it.
- Queue empties → -1.

- Every intermediate word must be in the dictionary. That is what makes it a graph search rather than a string-distance calculation.
- All words are the same length in the base problem. The third follow-up removes that.
- Every step costs 1, so BFS is optimal and Dijkstra is unnecessary.
- The dictionary can be large — tens of thousands of words — which is why the neighbour function, not the search, is the design problem.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `Dictionary<string, List<string>>` keyed on wildcard patterns | Turns neighbour generation from a dictionary scan into L hash lookups. The one-off build cost is paid back on the first query. |
| `HashSet<string>` with `StringComparer.Ordinal` | Ordinal comparison is both faster and *correct* here — culture-aware comparison can treat different strings as equal, which in a word-graph silently merges nodes. This is a real C# footgun and worth one sentence. |
| Level-by-level BFS rather than `(word, depth)` pairs | Less state, and `steps++` happens in exactly one place, which is where the edge-versus-word convention lives. |
| `HashSet` frontiers in the bidirectional version, not queues | A frontier has to be countable (to pick the smaller side) and membership-testable (to detect the meeting). A queue is neither. |
| `Index` as a separate method | So `AddWord` can reuse it. The dynamic-dictionary follow-up is then two lines instead of a redesign. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**Why `Index` reuses one `char[]` and restores it.** `chars[i] = '*'` then `chars[i] = keep`. Allocating a fresh array per position would be L times the garbage for no benefit. `new string(chars)` still allocates the pattern — unavoidable, since it is the dictionary key — but the buffer is reused. Small, and it is the difference between a build that scales and one that pressures the GC on a large dictionary.

**`StringComparer.Ordinal`, deliberately.** Passed to every `HashSet` and `Dictionary`. Without it, .NET uses the default comparer, and for strings the culture-sensitive paths can treat distinct sequences as equal. In a word graph that means two different words collapse into one node and the shortest path can come out wrong. It is also measurably faster.

**The neighbour function is an iterator.** `yield return` means the BFS stops as soon as it finds the end word, without materialising the rest of the neighbours. On a word with 100 neighbours where the second one is the target, that is 98 fewer set operations.

**`if (w != word)` inside the bucket.** A word is in its own wildcard buckets, so it would otherwise be its own neighbour. Harmless (the visited set catches it) and worth excluding anyway, because "a word is one change from itself" is not true and the code should not say it is.

**Why the end-word check is on discovery.** Returning `steps` the moment the end word is seen as a neighbour, rather than waiting to dequeue it, is what makes `steps` the edge count. `steps++` has already happened for this level, so it equals the number of edges traversed to reach the neighbour. Moving the check to the dequeue point without moving `steps++` gives an answer one too large — which, not coincidentally, is the LeetCode 127 answer.

**The bidirectional swap.** `(frontA, frontB) = (frontB, frontA);` together with `(seenA, seenB)`. Both must move, or the meeting test checks the wrong set. `steps++` once per round is still correct because each round lays down exactly one edge, whichever side expanded — and that is the part I would not trust by inspection, which is why 200 random pairs are cross-checked against plain BFS.

**`AddWord` is three lines.** `if (_words.Add(word)) Index(word);` — the dynamic-dictionary follow-up, for free, because indexing was factored out. Removal would be harder: it needs the word pulled from L buckets, so the buckets would want to be sets rather than lists.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| build | O(N · L²) | O(N · L²) | N words × L patterns, each pattern a string of length L |
| `MinTransformations` | O(V + E) worst case | O(N) | E is bounded by the total bucket sizes; each word is visited once |
| neighbours of one word | O(L + bucket sizes) | O(1) extra | L hash lookups instead of a dictionary scan |
| `MinTransformationsBidirectional` | O(b^(d/2)) typical | O(b^(d/2)) | Two shallow searches rather than one deep one |
| `AddWord` | O(L²) | O(L²) | L new pattern keys for one word |

**The build is O(N · L²), not O(N · L)** — each of the L patterns is itself a string of length L that has to be constructed and hashed. At N = 50,000 and L = 5 that is about 1.25 million character operations, which is nothing; at L = 20 it starts to matter, and a rolling hash would be the fix. Getting the L² right rather than saying L is a small piece of precision that is easy to be sloppy about.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Start equals end | 0, before any search. |
| Different lengths | -1. Single-character substitution cannot change length in the base problem. |
| End word not in the dictionary | -1, checked up front — otherwise the search runs to exhaustion for nothing. |
| Start word not in the dictionary | Allowed. Its neighbours still come from the buckets, which contain only real words, so the path is legal. |
| No path exists | -1 when the queue empties. The bidirectional version must exit when **either** frontier empties. |
| Empty dictionary | -1, via the end-word check. |
| Single-character words | Works; every word is one change from every other, so the answer is almost always 1. |
| Duplicate words in the input | `HashSet` de-duplicates, so buckets hold each word once. |
| Mixed case | Treated as distinct under ordinal comparison. Normalise at the boundary if that is wrong. |
| A very large bucket | A pattern like `*AT` can hold many words. That is the real branching factor, and it is the argument for searching from both ends. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Convert this to an online service with minimal latency.**

Four things, in order of payoff.

**Build the wildcard index once at startup**, not per request — that is already how the class is written, and it is the whole reason the constructor takes the dictionary.

**Use bidirectional BFS per query**, since it is the single biggest constant reduction available and the branching factor here is large.

**Cache answers.** Word pairs repeat heavily in any real workload, and the result is immutable for a fixed dictionary, so an LRU cache keyed on the unordered pair is a near-free win — which is Q1, and worth pointing out that the two questions compose.

**Shard by word length.** Words of different lengths can never be neighbours, so the graph is already partitioned. Each shard is independent, holds a smaller index, and can be served by a different process with no coordination at all.

*Trade-off:* Memory for latency, and staleness for speed. The index is roughly L² strings per word, so a 500,000-word dictionary at L = 8 is a real amount of memory and is the reason sharding by length is attractive. The cache introduces an invalidation problem the moment the dictionary changes — and since adding one word can shorten arbitrarily many paths, the honest answer is to version the dictionary and key the cache on the version, so an update invalidates everything at once rather than trying to be clever about which entries changed.

**Will cycles be output?**

**No, to both, and for the same reason.** The visited set means each word is enqueued at most once, so the search cannot loop. And BFS explores in order of increasing distance, so the first time it reaches a word is via a shortest path — a path that revisited a word would be strictly longer than the same path with the loop removed, so it can never be the one found.

The graph itself is full of cycles, of course. The point is that a shortest path in any graph is always simple, and BFS finds shortest paths.

*Trade-off:* None here — it is a property of the algorithm, not a design decision. Where it would matter is if you dropped the visited set to enumerate *all* paths: then cycles become possible and you need per-path tracking rather than a global set, and the cost goes exponential.

**What if letters can be added or removed?**

Adjacency becomes "edit distance exactly 1", so words of *different* lengths are now neighbours and the graph is no longer partitioned by length. BFS still applies; only the neighbour function changes.

The wildcard index needs a second half. For substitution, keep the existing `A*E`-style patterns. For insertion and deletion, index each word under every **deletion** of one character: `APE` also goes under `PE`, `AE`, `AP`. Then a word of length L and a word of length L+1 are neighbours exactly when the shorter one equals one of the longer one’s deletion patterns — so deletion neighbours are, again, hash lookups rather than comparisons.

*Trade-off:* The index roughly doubles, and the branching factor grows a lot, because a word is now adjacent to longer and shorter words as well. Length-based sharding is lost — which is a real cost, since it was the cleanest scaling axis. Bidirectional search becomes more valuable, not less, because b went up. If the question were the *distance* rather than the dictionary-constrained *path*, this stops being a graph problem and becomes the O(L¹ · L²) DP of LeetCode 72 — worth distinguishing the two out loud, because they sound the same and are not.

**Return the path, not just the length.**

A `Dictionary<string, string> parent` populated when a word is first discovered, walked back from the end word. For the bidirectional version, two parent maps joined at the meeting word, with one side reversed — and the meeting word belongs to both, so it must not be emitted twice.

*Trade-off:* O(N) extra memory, which is the same order as the visited set. Storing the whole path per frontier entry instead is the tempting shortcut and multiplies memory by the path length. If **all** shortest paths are wanted — which is LeetCode 126 — the parent becomes a list of parents and the reconstruction becomes a DFS over the resulting DAG, and the output can be exponentially large.

**The dictionary changes while the service is running.**

`AddWord` indexes the new word into its L buckets — already implemented, O(L²). Removal is harder: the word has to be pulled out of L buckets, and with `List<string>` buckets that is a linear scan of each. If removal matters, make the buckets `HashSet<string>` so it is O(L) instead.

The bigger problem is the cache. One added word can shorten unboundedly many paths, so there is no cheap partial invalidation — version the dictionary and key cached answers on the version.

*Trade-off:* `List` buckets are faster to build and to iterate, and slower to delete from. `HashSet` buckets are the opposite. Choose on the read/write ratio, which for a dictionary is overwhelmingly reads — so `List` is the right default and switching is the right answer only if removals are real.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**
